title: Physical premotion presupposes a moral motion through the object
source_text: LII. Quanquam vero istud auxilium efficax in motione quadam voluntatem physice praedeterminante constituant; agnoscunt tamen illud praesupponere motionem moralem, quae fit per objecti propositionem congruam, per quam apparet objectum illud amabile & conveniens voluntati. Nec enim voluntatem posse aliquid appetere, nisi prius per intellectum ei proponatur tanquam conveniens. Ac proinde neminem per auxilium gratiae physice determinari ad bonum prosequendum, quin mens ejus fuerit notitia istius boni illuminata, & voluntas ad illud appetendum invitata, & moraliter inclinata internis spiritus sancti suasionibus & suggestionibus. Verum inde nunquam consequitur, secundum illorum doctrinam, voluntatis consensus, nisi alterum illud auxilium accesserit, quod voluntatem ad consensum illum efficaciter & physice moveat.
pass_a_gloss: LII. But although they place that efficacious help in a certain motion physically predetermining the will; they acknowledge however that it presupposes a moral motion, which is done through a congruous proposal of the object, through which that object appears lovable and fitting to the will. For neither can the will desire anything, unless first through the intellect it be proposed to it as fitting. And therefore that no one through the help of grace is physically determined to pursuing good, without his mind having been illuminated by knowledge of that good, and the will invited to desiring it, and morally inclined by internal suasions and suggestions of the holy spirit. But from that never follows, according to their doctrine, the consent of the will, unless that other help be added, which moves the will to that consent efficaciously and physically.
pass_b_english: Thesis LII. Although they place this efficacious aid in a motion that physically predetermines the will, they acknowledge that it presupposes a moral motion, brought about by a fitting presentation of the object through which that object appears lovable and suited to the will. For the will cannot desire anything unless the intellect first presents it to the will as suited to it.

So no one is physically determined by the aid of grace to pursue the good unless his mind has been enlightened with knowledge of that good, and his will invited to desire it and morally inclined by the inward persuasions and promptings of the Holy Spirit. Yet on their teaching the will's consent never follows from this unless that other aid is added which moves the will effectively and physically to consent.

lemmas.gloss: through a congruous proposal of the object
by internal suasions and suggestions of the holy spirit

choices.why: Scholastic contrast: a physical motion works on the faculty itself; a moral motion works by attracting and persuading through the object (as XLII and LII explain).
